claim: CB1R is one of the most abundant G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in the CNS.
source: CB1R is one of the most abundant G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in the CNS and endocannabinoid signalling through CB1R is a neuromodulatory system that influences a wide range of brain functions including pain, appetite, mood, and memory (Soltesz et al., 2015; Lu and Mackie, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Soltesz et al., 2015; Lu and Mackie, 2016).

claim: Endocannabinoid signalling through CB1R influences pain, appetite, mood, and memory.
source: CB1R is one of the most abundant G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in the CNS and endocannabinoid signalling through CB1R is a neuromodulatory system that influences a wide range of brain functions including pain, appetite, mood, and memory (Soltesz et al., 2015; Lu and Mackie, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Soltesz et al., 2015; Lu and Mackie, 2016).

claim: CB1R function and dysfunction are implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Furthermore, CB1R function and dysfunction are implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders (Basavarajappa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Basavarajappa et al., 2017).

claim: Modulation of endocannabinoid pathways is of intense interest as a potential therapeutic target.
source: Thus, modulation of endocannabinoid pathways is of intense interest as a potential therapeutic target (Reddy, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Reddy, 2017).

claim: CB1R is present in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and also in astroglia.
source: CB1R is present in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and also in astroglia, where it plays important roles in synaptic plasticity and memory (Han et al., 2012; Robin et al., 2018; Busquets-Garcia et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Han et al., 2012; Robin et al., 2018; Busquets-Garcia et al., 2018).

claim: CB1R plays important roles in synaptic plasticity and memory.
source: CB1R is present in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and also in astroglia, where it plays important roles in synaptic plasticity and memory (Han et al., 2012; Robin et al., 2018; Busquets-Garcia et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Han et al., 2012; Robin et al., 2018; Busquets-Garcia et al., 2018).

claim: In hippocampal neurons, ~80% of CB1R is present in intracellular vesicular clusters in the soma and dendrites.
source: In hippocampal neurons, ~80% of CB1R is present in intracellular vesicular clusters in the soma and dendrites (Leterrier et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Leterrier et al., 2006).

claim: CB1R is not stably surface expressed on somatodendritic plasma membrane.
source: Strikingly, however, CB1R is not stably surface expressed on somatodendritic plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the manuscript's experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: CB1R has a highly polarised axonal surface expression.
source: Rather, it has a highly polarised axonal surface expression (Irving et al., 2000; Coutts et al., 2001) where it acts to attenuate neurotransmitter release (Katona, 2009) and modulate synaptic plasticity (Lu and Mackie, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Irving et al., 2000; Coutts et al., 2001).

claim: CB1R acts to attenuate neurotransmitter release.
source: Rather, it has a highly polarised axonal surface expression (Irving et al., 2000; Coutts et al., 2001) where it acts to attenuate neurotransmitter release (Katona, 2009) and modulate synaptic plasticity (Lu and Mackie, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Katona, 2009).

claim: CB1R modulates synaptic plasticity.
source: Rather, it has a highly polarised axonal surface expression (Irving et al., 2000; Coutts et al., 2001) where it acts to attenuate neurotransmitter release (Katona, 2009) and modulate synaptic plasticity (Lu and Mackie, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lu and Mackie, 2016).

claim: High rates of endocytosis due to constitutive activity selectively remove CB1Rs from the somatodendritic plasma membrane, resulting in an accumulation at the axonal surface.
source: One suggestion is that high rates of endocytosis due to constitutive activity selectively remove CB1Rs from the somatodendritic plasma membrane, resulting in an accumulation at the axonal surface (Leterrier et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Leterrier et al., 2006) and represents a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: Internalised somatodendritic CB1Rs may be either sorted for degradation or recycled to axons via a transcytotic sorting pathway.
source: These internalised somatodendritic CB1Rs may then be either sorted for degradation or recycled to axons via a transcytotic sorting pathway (Simon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Simon et al., 2013) and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Newly synthesized CB1Rs may be constitutively targeted to lysosomes, but under appropriate circumstances the CB1Rs destined for degradation are retrieved and rerouted to axons.
source: Alternatively, newly synthesized CB1Rs may be constitutively targeted to lysosomes, but under appropriate circumstances the CB1Rs destined for degradation are retrieved and rerouted to axons (Rozenfeld and Devi, 2008; Rozenfeld, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Rozenfeld and Devi, 2008; Rozenfeld, 2011) and represents an alternative hypothesis.

claim: A direct role for the 73-residue intracellular C-terminal domain of CB1R (ctCB1R) in axonal/somatodendritic trafficking or polarised surface expression has not been identified.
source: Surprisingly, a direct role for the 73-residue intracellular C-terminal domain of CB1R (ctCB1R) in axonal/somatodendritic trafficking or polarised surface expression has not been identified.
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior findings in the literature as stated by the authors.

claim: Motifs within ctCB1R are required for receptor desensitization and internalization.
source: It has, however, been reported that motifs within ctCB1R are required for receptor desensitization and internalization (Hsieh et al., 1999; Jin et al., 1999) (reviewed by Mackie, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hsieh et al., 1999; Jin et al., 1999) and a review (Mackie, 2008).

claim: There are two putative amphipathic helical domains in ctCB1R (H8 and H9).
source: Interestingly, there are two putative amphipathic helical domains in ctCB1R (H8 and H9 [Ahn et al., 2009]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ahn et al., 2009).

claim: H8 has been proposed to play a role in ER assembly and/or exit during biosynthesis.
source: H8 has been proposed to play a role in ER assembly and/or exit during biosynthesis (Ahn et al., 2010; Stadel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ahn et al., 2010; Stadel et al., 2011).

claim: The role of the 21-residue H9 motif is unknown.
source: The role of the 21-residue H9 motif is unknown, although analogous regions have been reported to act as a Gαq-binding site in both squid rhodopsin (Murakami and Kouyama, 2008) and bradykinin receptors (Piserchio et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on the absence of prior findings in the literature as stated by the authors.

claim: Analogous regions to H9 have been reported to act as a Gαq-binding site in both squid rhodopsin and bradykinin receptors.
source: The role of the 21-residue H9 motif is unknown, although analogous regions have been reported to act as a Gαq-binding site in both squid rhodopsin (Murakami and Kouyama, 2008) and bradykinin receptors (Piserchio et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Murakami and Kouyama, 2008) and (Piserchio et al., 2005).

claim: A population of CB1R is preferentially targeted to the axon through the biosynthetic pathway.
source: We demonstrate that a population of CB1R is preferentially targeted to the axon through the biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RUSH experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1Rs that reach the dendritic membrane are rapidly removed by endocytosis.
source: CB1Rs that reach the dendritic membrane are rapidly removed by endocytosis whereas CB1Rs surface expressed on the axonal membrane have a longer residence time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antibody feeding experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1Rs surface expressed on the axonal membrane have a longer residence time.
source: CB1Rs that reach the dendritic membrane are rapidly removed by endocytosis whereas CB1Rs surface expressed on the axonal membrane have a longer residence time.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antibody feeding experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The putative helical domain H9 in ctCB1R plays a key role in CB1R surface expression and endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
source: We further show that the putative helical domain H9 in ctCB1R plays a key role in CB1R surface expression and endocytosis in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing CB1RWT and CB1RΔH9 presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1R polarity is determined, at least in part, by a novel determinant in the C-terminus of CB1R that contributes to targeted delivery to the axonal compartment.
source: Taken together our data suggest that CB1R polarity is determined, at least in part, by a novel determinant in the C-terminus of CB1R that contributes to targeted delivery to the axonal compartment and the rapid removal of CB1Rs that reach the somatodendritic membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The C-terminus of CB1R contributes to the rapid removal of CB1Rs that reach the somatodendritic membrane.
source: Taken together our data suggest that CB1R polarity is determined, at least in part, by a novel determinant in the C-terminus of CB1R that contributes to targeted delivery to the axonal compartment and the rapid removal of CB1Rs that reach the somatodendritic membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Prior to biotin-mediated release, SBP-EGFP-CB1R was retained in the ER in the soma and dendrites but was absent from the axonal compartment and was not present at the cell surface.
source: Prior to biotin-mediated release, SBP-EGFP-CB1R was retained in the ER in the soma and dendrites but was absent from the axonal compartment and was not present at the cell surface (0 min; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After addition of biotin, SBP-EGFP-CB1R moved through the secretory pathway and entered the proximal segment of the axonal compartment at 25 min.
source: After addition of biotin, SBP-EGFP-CB1R moved through the secretory pathway and entered the proximal segment of the axonal compartment at 25 min and continued to accumulate until 45 min when it reached its peak, which was comparable to an unretained control (O/N) (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: SBP-EGFP-CB1R continued to accumulate until 45 min when it reached its peak, which was comparable to an unretained control.
source: After addition of biotin, SBP-EGFP-CB1R moved through the secretory pathway and entered the proximal segment of the axonal compartment at 25 min and continued to accumulate until 45 min when it reached its peak, which was comparable to an unretained control (O/N) (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Once released from the ER, CB1R is immediately trafficked towards the axonal compartment, and passes through the axon initial segment (AIS) via the intracellular secretory pathway.
source: These data suggest that once released from the ER, CB1R is immediately trafficked towards the axonal compartment, and passes through the axon initial segment (AIS), which constitutes an exclusion and diffusion barrier to separate the axonal from the somatodendritic compartments, via the intracellular secretory pathway.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: SBP-EGFP-CB1R was surface expressed in the proximal segment of axons 40 min after release from the ER.
source: SBP-EGFP-CB1R was surface expressed in the proximal segment of axons 40 min after release from the ER, whereas in dendrites, CB1R was not surface expressed until 60 min after release (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In dendrites, CB1R was not surface expressed until 60 min after release from the ER.
source: SBP-EGFP-CB1R was surface expressed in the proximal segment of axons 40 min after release from the ER, whereas in dendrites, CB1R was not surface expressed until 60 min after release (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Significantly more SBP-EGFP-CB1R reached the surface of axons than the surface of dendrites 45, 60, and 90 min after release from the ER.
source: Moreover, significantly more SBP-EGFP-CB1R reached the surface of axons than the surface of dendrites 45, 60, and 90 min after release from the ER (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: The secretory pathway delivers a greater amount of CB1R more rapidly to the axonal membrane than to the dendritic membrane.
source: These data demonstrate that the secretory pathway delivers a greater amount of CB1R more rapidly to the axonal membrane than to the dendritic membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: In the proximal segment of axons, most surface expressed SBP-EGFP-CB1R is stable and retained at the axonal membrane.
source: In the proximal segment of axons, the normalised surface and surface + endocytosed curves were identical, suggesting that most surface expressed SBP-EGFP-CB1R is stable and retained at the axonal membrane (Figure 2D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2F.

claim: In dendrites there is significantly less surface than surface + endocytosed SBP-EGFP-CB1R 90 min after addition of biotin.
source: In stark contrast, however, in dendrites there is significantly less surface than surface + endocytosed SBP-EGFP-CB1R 90 min after addition of biotin, indicating that surface expressed CB1R is more rapidly endocytosed from and/or not recycled back to the dendritic membrane (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G with statistical analysis.

claim: Surface expressed CB1R is more rapidly endocytosed from and/or not recycled back to the dendritic membrane.
source: In stark contrast, however, in dendrites there is significantly less surface than surface + endocytosed SBP-EGFP-CB1R 90 min after addition of biotin, indicating that surface expressed CB1R is more rapidly endocytosed from and/or not recycled back to the dendritic membrane (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: By 30 min after release from the ER, and before CB1R appears on the surface, intracellular CB1R has progressed through the AIS and is already present at least 100 µm along the axon at levels similar to the unretained control.
source: Analysis of CB1R total fluorescence along the axon indicates that by 30 min after release from the ER, and before CB1R appears on the surface, intracellular CB1R has progressed through the AIS and is already present at least 100 µm along the axon at levels similar to the unretained control (O/N; Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: CB1R-containing secretory vesicles can rapidly travel to more distal areas of the axon.
source: These data indicate that CB1R-containing secretory vesicles can rapidly travel to more distal areas of the axon.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2H and 2I.

claim: Surface CB1Rs delivered from the secretory pathway accumulate at the final portion of the AIS, before then progressing further along the axon.
source: Furthermore, surface CB1Rs delivered from the secretory pathway accumulate at the final portion of the AIS, before then progressing further along the axon (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CB1R surface polarity is initially established and maintained by two distinct but complementary mechanisms.
source: Our results using RUSH time-resolved analysis show that CB1R surface polarity is initially established and maintained by two distinct but complementary mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The secretory pathway preferentially delivers CB1R to the axonal surface, with significantly less going to the dendritic surface.
source: Firstly, we show the novel finding that the secretory pathway preferentially delivers CB1R to the axonal surface, with significantly less going to the dendritic surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RUSH experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Newly delivered CB1R is preferentially retained/stabilised at the axonal membrane and internalised from the dendritic membrane.
source: Secondly, by distinguishing between surface and surface + endocytosed receptors, our antibody feeding experiments show that newly delivered CB1R is preferentially retained/stabilised at the axonal membrane and internalised from the dendritic membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antibody feeding experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differential internalisation of CB1R is due to the presence of agonist in the dendritic membrane and absence of agonist on axonal membrane.
source: Previous literature proposes that this differential internalisation is due to the presence of agonist in the dendritic membrane and absence of agonist on axonal membrane (Leterrier et al., 2006; Ladarre et al., 2014), although a potential role for constitutive internalisation distinct to agonist-induced internalisation has also been proposed (McDonald et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Leterrier et al., 2006; Ladarre et al., 2014).

claim: Preferential delivery to the proximal segment of the axon and less rapid internalisation of axonally surface expressed CB1Rs are major contributors to the axonal surface polarisation of CB1R in hippocampal neurons.
source: Taken together, we propose that preferential delivery to the proximal segment of the axon and less rapid internalisation of axonally surface expressed CB1Rs are major contributors to the axonal surface polarisation of CB1R in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CD4-ctCB1RWT was markedly more axonally polarised than CD4 alone.
source: Analysis of the axon to dendrite ratio of surface expression (the surface polarity index) revealed that CD4-ctCB1RWT was markedly more axonally polarised than CD4 alone, indicating that ctCB1R may play a role in polarisation despite its lack of defined canonical localisation signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: ctCB1R may play a role in polarisation despite its lack of defined canonical localisation signals.
source: Analysis of the axon to dendrite ratio of surface expression (the surface polarity index) revealed that CD4-ctCB1RWT was markedly more axonally polarised than CD4 alone, indicating that ctCB1R may play a role in polarisation despite its lack of defined canonical localisation signals.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The degree of polarisation was significantly lower for CD4-ctCB1RΔH9 compared to CD4-ctCB1RWT.
source: Moreover, although still significantly axonally polarised, the degree of polarisation was significantly lower for CD4-ctCB1RΔH9, suggesting that H9 may also contribute to this process (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: H9 may contribute to CB1R polarisation.
source: Moreover, although still significantly axonally polarised, the degree of polarisation was significantly lower for CD4-ctCB1RΔH9, suggesting that H9 may also contribute to this process (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: H9 does not determine surface polarity by driving differential constitutive endocytosis from either the dendritic or axonal membrane.
source: H9 does not determine surface polarity by driving differential constitutive endocytosis from either the dendritic or axonal membrane since there was no difference between the internalisation of CD4-ctCB1RWT or CD4-ctCB1RΔH9.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both CD4-ctCB1RWT and CD4-ctCB1RΔH9 were significantly more internalised than CD4 alone in dendrites, but not in axons.
source: Interestingly, both CD4-ctCB1RWT and CD4-ctCB1RΔH9 were significantly more internalised than CD4 alone in dendrites, but not in axons (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and 4B with statistical analysis.

claim: A domain other than H9 promotes constitutive, but reportedly not activity-dependent, internalisation in dendrites.
source: These results suggest that a domain other than H9 promotes constitutive, but reportedly not activity-dependent (McDonald et al., 2007a), internalisation in dendrites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4 and a citation to published literature (McDonald et al., 2007a).

claim: Significantly more SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 than SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT reached the surface of dendrites during the time course of the experiments.
source: Interestingly, significantly more SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 than SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT reached the surface of dendrites during the time course of our experiments (Figure 5B), whereas trafficking to axons was similar for both SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claim: Trafficking to axons was similar for both SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9.
source: Interestingly, significantly more SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 than SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT reached the surface of dendrites during the time course of our experiments (Figure 5B), whereas trafficking to axons was similar for both SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: H9 plays a role in restricting delivery of CB1R to the dendritic membrane.
source: These altered properties resulted in a significant difference in the surface + endocytosed polarity index after 90 min (Figure 5D) and are consistent with a role for H9 in restricting delivery of CB1R to the dendritic membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The polarity of the amount of CB1R on the cell surface 90 min after biotin-mediated release was identical for SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9.
source: Surprisingly, in contrast to the total amount of CB1R that had been surface expressed during the time course (surface + endocytosed; Figure 5D), the polarity of the amount of CB1R on the cell surface 90 min after biotin-mediated release was identical for SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 (surface; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At 90 min there is significantly less surface expression of SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 than SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT in axons.
source: However, at 90 min there is significantly less surface expression of ΔH9 mutant (Figure 5F) suggesting that, although similar amounts of SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 reach the surface, surface expression of SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 is less stable than that of the wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F with statistical analysis.

claim: Surface expression of SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 is less stable than that of the wild-type.
source: However, at 90 min there is significantly less surface expression of ΔH9 mutant (Figure 5F) suggesting that, although similar amounts of SBP-EGFP-CB1RWT and SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 reach the surface, surface expression of SBP-EGFP-CB1RΔH9 is less stable than that of the wild-type.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In dendrites, the increased delivery and surface trafficking of the ΔH9 mutant is counteracted by the fact that less is retained at the surface 60 min after ER release.
source: Furthermore, in dendrites, the increased delivery and surface trafficking of the ΔH9 mutant is counteracted by the fact that less is retained at the surface 60 min after ER release (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G with statistical analysis.

claim: H9 plays a role in membrane stability and retention at both axons and dendrites.
source: Taken together these results suggest that, separate from its role in restricting delivery to the dendritic membrane, H9 also plays a role in membrane stability and retention at both axons and dendrites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed lower levels of surface expression in both axons and dendrites compared to EGFP-CB1RWT.
source: EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed lower levels of surface expression (Figure 6C), as well as increased endocytosis (Figure 6D) in both axons and dendrites compared to EGFP-CB1RWT, suggesting H9 plays a role in stabilising CB1R at the surface of both axons and dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claim: EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed increased endocytosis in both axons and dendrites compared to EGFP-CB1RWT.
source: EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed lower levels of surface expression (Figure 6C), as well as increased endocytosis (Figure 6D) in both axons and dendrites compared to EGFP-CB1RWT, suggesting H9 plays a role in stabilising CB1R at the surface of both axons and dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D with statistical analysis.

claim: H9 plays a role in stabilising CB1R at the surface of both axons and dendrites.
source: EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed lower levels of surface expression (Figure 6C), as well as increased endocytosis (Figure 6D) in both axons and dendrites compared to EGFP-CB1RWT, suggesting H9 plays a role in stabilising CB1R at the surface of both axons and dendrites.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: There was no difference in surface polarity between EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 at steady-state.
source: Moreover, similar to our findings using RUSH, there was no difference in surface polarity between EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: While H9 plays a role in CB1R surface expression and endocytosis, its potential to mediate surface polarity is masked in the full-length receptor.
source: These results suggest that, while H9 plays a role in CB1R surface expression and endocytosis, its potential to mediate surface polarity is masked in the full-length receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: There was no significant difference in ERK1/2 phosphorylation in cells expressing EGFP-CB1RWT or EGFP-CB1RΔH9 under basal conditions in the absence of ACEA.
source: There was no significant difference in ERK1/2 phosphorylation in cells expressing EGFP-CB1RWT or EGFP-CB1RΔH9 under basal conditions in the absence of ACEA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Upon ACEA stimulation, the level of ERK1/2 activation was significantly reduced in EGFP-CB1RΔH9-transfected cells compared to EGFP-CB1RWT-transfected cells expressing equivalent amounts of receptor.
source: However, upon ACEA stimulation, the level of ERK1/2 activation was significantly reduced in EGFP-CB1RΔH9-transfected cells compared to EGFP-CB1RWT-transfected cells expressing equivalent amounts of receptor (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C with statistical analysis.

claim: EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 were surface expressed at equivalent levels in HEK293T cells.
source: However, EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 were surface expressed at equivalent levels in HEK293T cells, as determined by surface biotinylation experiments (Figure 7D–E), suggesting the ΔH9 mutant is deficient in its ability to activate downstream signalling pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: The ΔH9 mutant is deficient in its ability to activate downstream signalling pathways.
source: However, EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 were surface expressed at equivalent levels in HEK293T cells, as determined by surface biotinylation experiments (Figure 7D–E), suggesting the ΔH9 mutant is deficient in its ability to activate downstream signalling pathways.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: ACEA-induced internalisation of EGFP-CB1RΔH9 was significantly greater than that observed for EGFP-CB1RWT in axons of hippocampal neurons.
source: ACEA-induced internalisation of EGFP-CB1RΔH9 was significantly greater than that observed for EGFP-CB1RWT (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and 7G with statistical analysis.

claim: CB1RΔH9 is less stable at the axonal surface under basal conditions.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that CB1RΔH9 is less stable at the axonal surface under basal conditions and that it is more susceptible to agonist-induced internalisation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: CB1RΔH9 is more susceptible to agonist-induced internalisation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that CB1RΔH9 is less stable at the axonal surface under basal conditions and that it is more susceptible to agonist-induced internalisation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: In hippocampal neurons treated with the DMSO control both EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed similar levels of surface polarity.
source: In hippocampal neurons treated with the DMSO control both EGFP-CB1RWT and EGFP-CB1RΔH9 displayed similar levels of surface polarity (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the presence of AM281, EGFP-CB1RΔH9 had significantly reduced surface polarity compared EGFP-CB1RWT.
source: In the presence of AM281, however, EGFP-CB1RΔH9 had significantly reduced surface polarity compared EGFP-CB1RWT (Figure 8B) due to a significantly increased amount of dendritic surface expression (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B with statistical analysis.

claim: In the presence of AM281, significantly more EGFP-CB1RΔH9 than EGFP-CB1RWT relocated to the surface of dendrites.
source: In the presence of AM281, however, EGFP-CB1RΔH9 had significantly reduced surface polarity compared EGFP-CB1RWT (Figure 8B) due to a significantly increased amount of dendritic surface expression (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C with statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of constitutive activity of the receptor, H9 plays a role in mediating CB1R surface polarity.
source: These results indicate that in the absence of constitutive activity of the receptor, H9 plays a role in mediating CB1R surface polarity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The increased internalisation observed in dendrites with H9 deletion may be mediated by the presence of endogenous agonist.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that the increased internalisation observed in dendrites with H9 deletion may be mediated by the presence of endogenous agonist and reaffirm the importance of the neuronal milieu on CB1R trafficking.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Two distinct, but complementary, mechanisms contribute to the polarisation of CB1Rs.
source: As illustrated in schematic form in Figure 9, our data indicate that two distinct, but complementary, mechanisms contribute to this polarisation of CB1Rs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: More de novo CB1R is delivered to the axon and it is more rapidly surface expressed than in dendrites.
source: 1) Using time-resolved RUSH assays we demonstrate that more de novo CB1R is delivered to the axon and that it is more rapidly surface expressed than in dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RUSH experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Once at the axonal membrane the newly delivered CB1R is more stably retained whereas in dendritic membrane CB1R surface expression is transient and it is rapidly internalised.
source: 2) Once at the axonal membrane the newly delivered CB1R is more stably retained whereas in dendritic membrane CB1R surface expression is transient and it is rapidly internalised.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antibody feeding experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1R internalised in the somatodendritic compartment can be rerouted to the axon via the transcytosis pathway.
source: It should be noted, however, that our data do not exclude additional possibilities, including that CB1R internalised in the somatodendritic compartment can be rerouted to the axon via the transcytosis pathway, thus further facilitating axonal polarity (Simon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Simon et al., 2013) and represents a possibility not excluded by the current data.

claim: CD4-ctCB1RWT and CD4-ctCB1RΔH9 chimeras cannot bind agonist.
source: Furthermore, since CD4-ctCB1RWT and CD4-ctCB1RΔH9 chimeras cannot bind agonist, our results are consistent with ctCB1R contributing to constitutive polarisation via a mechanism distinct from the proposed continuous activation of CB1R by the presence of the endogenous agonist 2-Arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) in the dendritic membrane (Ladarre et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of CD4 structure and function, as CD4 lacks the agonist binding domain of CB1R.

claim: ctCB1R contributes to constitutive polarisation via a mechanism distinct from the proposed continuous activation of CB1R by the presence of the endogenous agonist 2-Arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) in the dendritic membrane.
source: Furthermore, since CD4-ctCB1RWT and CD4-ctCB1RΔH9 chimeras cannot bind agonist, our results are consistent with ctCB1R contributing to constitutive polarisation via a mechanism distinct from the proposed continuous activation of CB1R by the presence of the endogenous agonist 2-Arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) in the dendritic membrane (Ladarre et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data with CD4 chimeras and a citation to published literature (Ladarre et al., 2014).

claim: ctCB1R contributes to the constitutive preferential delivery of CB1R to the axonal membrane.
source: Thus, we conclude that ctCB1R contributes to the constitutive preferential delivery of CB1R to the axonal membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ctCB1R is important for maintaining axonal surface polarity, in part mediated by the H9 motif.
source: Our results further demonstrate that ctCB1R is important for maintaining axonal surface polarity, in part mediated by the H9 motif, which plays a role in both the preferential delivery and selective retention of CB1R at in axons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The H9 motif plays a role in both the preferential delivery and selective retention of CB1R in axons.
source: Our results further demonstrate that ctCB1R is important for maintaining axonal surface polarity, in part mediated by the H9 motif, which plays a role in both the preferential delivery and selective retention of CB1R at in axons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1RΔH9 lacks the preferential delivery to axons observed for CB1RWT.
source: More specifically, these include; i) CB1RΔH9 lacks the preferential delivery to axons observed for CB1RWT, ii) CB1RΔH9 is less efficiently surface expressed, iii) CB1RΔH9 that does reach the surface it is more rapidly endocytosed in both axons and dendrites, and iv) CB1RΔH9 is more sensitive to agonist-induced internalisation and less efficient at downstream signalling, monitored by activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RUSH experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1RΔH9 is less efficiently surface expressed.
source: More specifically, these include; i) CB1RΔH9 lacks the preferential delivery to axons observed for CB1RWT, ii) CB1RΔH9 is less efficiently surface expressed, iii) CB1RΔH9 that does reach the surface it is more rapidly endocytosed in both axons and dendrites, and iv) CB1RΔH9 is more sensitive to agonist-induced internalisation and less efficient at downstream signalling, monitored by activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1RΔH9 that does reach the surface is more rapidly endocytosed in both axons and dendrites.
source: More specifically, these include; i) CB1RΔH9 lacks the preferential delivery to axons observed for CB1RWT, ii) CB1RΔH9 is less efficiently surface expressed, iii) CB1RΔH9 that does reach the surface it is more rapidly endocytosed in both axons and dendrites, and iv) CB1RΔH9 is more sensitive to agonist-induced internalisation and less efficient at downstream signalling, monitored by activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1RΔH9 is more sensitive to agonist-induced internalisation.
source: More specifically, these include; i) CB1RΔH9 lacks the preferential delivery to axons observed for CB1RWT, ii) CB1RΔH9 is less efficiently surface expressed, iii) CB1RΔH9 that does reach the surface it is more rapidly endocytosed in both axons and dendrites, and iv) CB1RΔH9 is more sensitive to agonist-induced internalisation and less efficient at downstream signalling, monitored by activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CB1RΔH9 is less efficient at downstream signalling, monitored by activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
source: More specifically, these include; i) CB1RΔH9 lacks the preferential delivery to axons observed for CB1RWT, ii) CB1RΔH9 is less efficiently surface expressed, iii) CB1RΔH9 that does reach the surface it is more rapidly endocytosed in both axons and dendrites, and iv) CB1RΔH9 is more sensitive to agonist-induced internalisation and less efficient at downstream signalling, monitored by activation of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sorting of cargos to axons or dendrites depends on binding to different types of clathrin-associated adaptor proteins (AP); axonal cargo bind to AP-3 whereas dendritic cargo bind to AP-1.
source: For example, a recent study in C. elegans has suggested that sorting of cargos to axons or dendrites depends on binding to different types of clathrin-associated adaptor proteins (AP); axonal cargo bind to AP-3 whereas dendritic cargo bind to AP-1 (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Li et al., 2016).

claim: AP-3 binding has been associated with CB1R trafficking to the lysosome in the dendritic compartment.
source: Interestingly, AP-3 binding has been associated with CB1R trafficking to the lysosome in the dendritic compartment (Rozenfeld and Devi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Rozenfeld and Devi, 2008).

claim: H9 may modulate CB1R binding to AP-3, allowing for preferential delivery to axons and sorting to dendritic lysosomes.
source: One possibility is that H9 may modulate CB1R binding to AP-3, allowing for preferential delivery to axons and sorting to dendritic lysosomes, causing an decrease in dendritic membrane CB1R.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: CB1R polarisation was initiated in the first 90 min since they were directly targeted to, and surface expressed within, proximal axonal regions.
source: Our data show that CB1R polarisation was initiated in the first 90 min since they were directly targeted to, and surface expressed within, proximal axonal regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RUSH experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Immunocytochemistry in brain sections using immunogold electron microscopy or STORM super-resolution imaging detect CB1R predominantly at the presynaptic terminal.
source: Immunocytochemistry in brain sections using immunogold electron microscopy (Katona et al., 1999; Nyíri et al., 2005) or STORM super-resolution imaging (Dudok et al., 2015) detect CB1R predominantly at the presynaptic terminal, consistent with a disto-proximal gradient of expression at the axonal plasma membrane (Simon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Katona et al., 1999; Nyíri et al., 2005; Dudok et al., 2015).

claim: CB1Rs are highly mobile and diffuse rapidly in the plasma membrane.
source: CB1Rs are highly mobile and diffuse rapidly in the plasma membrane (Mikasova et al., 2008; Oddi et al., 2012), so the accumulation of surface CB1R we observe may be followed by lateral diffusion and 'capture' of surface CB1R at presynaptic sites, analogous to the diffusion and retention models proposed for AMPARs and GABAARs at the postsynaptic membrane (Hastings and Man, 2018; Kneussel and Hausrat, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mikasova et al., 2008; Oddi et al., 2012).

claim: The accumulation of surface CB1R may be followed by lateral diffusion and 'capture' of surface CB1R at presynaptic sites.
source: CB1Rs are highly mobile and diffuse rapidly in the plasma membrane (Mikasova et al., 2008; Oddi et al., 2012), so the accumulation of surface CB1R we observe may be followed by lateral diffusion and 'capture' of surface CB1R at presynaptic sites, analogous to the diffusion and retention models proposed for AMPARs and GABAARs at the postsynaptic membrane (Hastings and Man, 2018; Kneussel and Hausrat, 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: CB1R in somatodendritic endosomes can be rerouted and trafficked to distal axonal surfaces.
source: Indeed, it has been reported that CB1R in somatodendritic endosomes can be rerouted and trafficked to distal axonal surfaces (Simon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Simon et al., 2013).

claim: Intracellular CB1R is present at least 100 µm along the axon before it appears at the surface.
source: Our observation that intracellular CB1R is present at least 100 µm along the axon before it appears at the surface supports the concept of a rapid and direct trafficking of CB1R-containing secretory vesicles to more distal areas of the axon, although more detailed tracking of these secretory vesicles to presynaptic boutons would be required to confirm this.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Arrival at, and progression through, the AIS constitutes the initial phase of CB1R axonal polarisation.
source: Overall, we interpret our data to suggest that arrival at, and progression through, the AIS constitutes the initial phase of CB1R axonal polarisation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Once within the axonal compartment trafficking to more distal locations and to presynaptic sites is then mediated by additional mechanisms that probably include both intracellular transport and lateral diffusion and trapping.
source: Once within the axonal compartment trafficking to more distal locations and to presynaptic sites is then mediated by additional mechanisms that probably include both intracellular transport and lateral diffusion and trapping.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: H9 stabilises CB1R at the membrane, regardless of compartment.
source: Our data suggest that H9 stabilises CB1R at the membrane, regardless of compartment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Structural domains analogous to H9 have only been reported in squid rhodopsin and the bradykinin receptor.
source: While the H8 domain is highly conserved in GPCRs, structural domains analogous to H9 have only been reported in squid rhodopsin (Murakami and Kouyama, 2008) and the bradykinin receptor (Piserchio et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Murakami and Kouyama, 2008) and (Piserchio et al., 2005).

claim: H9, like H8, is an amphipathic α-helix, associating with the lipid bilayer via a cluster of hydrophobic residues on the non-polar face of the helix.
source: NMR and circular dichroism studies suggest that H9, like H8, is an amphipathic α-helix, associating with the lipid bilayer via a cluster of hydrophobic residues on the non-polar face of the helix (Ahn et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ahn et al., 2009).

claim: CB1R has been shown to be palmitoylated just downstream of H8 at C416, which affects its membrane association and G-protein coupling.
source: Furthermore, CB1R has been shown to be palmitoylated just downstream of H8 at C416, which affects its membrane association and G-protein coupling (Oddi et al., 2012; Oddi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Oddi et al., 2012; Oddi et al., 2018).

claim: H9 contains a cysteine residue.
source: H9 also contains a cysteine residue, raising the possibility that post-translational modifications such as palmitoylation, prenylation, or farnesylation at this site could modulate membrane association.
evidence: This claim is supported by the amino acid sequence shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Post-translational modifications such as palmitoylation, prenylation, or farnesylation at the cysteine in H9 could modulate membrane association.
source: H9 also contains a cysteine residue, raising the possibility that post-translational modifications such as palmitoylation, prenylation, or farnesylation at this site could modulate membrane association.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the presence of a cysteine residue in H9.

claim: The membrane association of H9 could mask internalisation signals or interacting motifs.
source: Since our data suggest that H9 stabilises CB1R at the membrane, it is possible that the membrane association of H9 could mask internalisation signals or interacting motifs.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: SGIP1, a protein linked to clathrin-mediated endocytosis, binds at an as yet undefined site on ctCB1R downstream of H8, preventing internalisation of activated CB1R.
source: For example, SGIP1, a protein linked to clathrin-mediated endocytosis, binds at an as yet undefined site on ctCB1R downstream of H8, preventing internalisation of activated CB1R (Hájková et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hájková et al., 2016).

claim: CRIP1a interacts directly with a motif in the last 9 C-terminal amino acids of CB1R.
source: Similarly, cannabinoid receptor interacting protein 1a (CRIP1a), which interacts directly with a motif in the last 9 C-terminal amino acids (Niehaus et al., 2007), reduces constitutive CB1R internalisation (Mascia et al., 2017) by competing with β-Arrestin binding (Blume et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Niehaus et al., 2007).

claim: CRIP1a reduces constitutive CB1R internalisation by competing with β-Arrestin binding.
source: Similarly, cannabinoid receptor interacting protein 1a (CRIP1a), which interacts directly with a motif in the last 9 C-terminal amino acids (Niehaus et al., 2007), reduces constitutive CB1R internalisation (Mascia et al., 2017) by competing with β-Arrestin binding (Blume et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mascia et al., 2017; Blume et al., 2017).

claim: H9 may mediate the interactions between CB1R and SGIP1 and/or selectively promote β-Arrestin rather than CRIP1a binding.
source: Therefore, it is possible that H9 mediates the interactions between CB1R and SGIP1 and/or selectively promotes β-Arrestin rather than CRIP1a binding.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: The C-terminal domain, and H9 in particular, play important roles in trafficking of CB1R.
source: Taken together, our results reveal that the C-terminal domain, and H9 in particular, play important roles in trafficking of CB1R.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: H9 is an important regulator of CB1R endocytosis and surface expression.
source: These findings provide important insight into the mechanisms of CB1R polarity and highlight H9 as an important regulator of CB1R endocytosis and surface expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
